description: Fact-check judge regression set (S2, 2026-11-25). 'recorded' pairs are our fact statements and the blind statements a third provider gave in the S3-A fact-check run; 'made' pairs are written to differ in meaning and must always be refused. Maths facts only, no personal data.

cases.a: tan x = sin x / cos x, and cos 90° = 0, so tan 90° is undefined.
cases.b: tan x is undefined at x = 90° for angles between 0° and 180°. This is because tan x = sin x / cos x, and cos 90° = 0, so the expression involves division by zero.

cases.a: Two straight lines are parallel exactly when they have the same gradient.
cases.b: For two non-vertical straight lines, the lines are parallel if and only if their gradients are equal: if the gradients are m1 and m2, then parallel implies m1 = m2 (and distinct parallel lines also have different intercepts).

cases.a: The graph of y = f(-x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in the y-axis.
cases.b: The graph of y = f(-x) is obtained by reflecting the graph of y = f(x) in the y-axis. This is because each point (x, f(x)) on the original graph becomes (-x, f(x)) on the new graph.

cases.a: The graph of y = -f(x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in the x-axis.
cases.b: The graph of y = -f(x) is obtained by reflecting the graph of y = f(x) in the x-axis. Equivalently, each point (x, y) maps to (x, -y).

cases.a: The area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled (for motion in one direction).
cases.b: The signed area under a velocity–time graph between two times represents the displacement over that time interval. If the graph stays above the time axis, this is also the distance travelled; if it goes below, areas below the axis count as negative displacement.

cases.a: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
cases.b: The gradient of a velocity–time graph represents the acceleration, i.e. the rate of change of velocity with respect to time. For a curved graph, the gradient at a point gives the instantaneous acceleration; for a straight-line section, the constant gradient gives the constant acceleration over that interval.

cases.a: The graph of y = f(x) + a is the graph of y = f(x) translated a units up (down if a is negative).
cases.b: The graph of y = f(x) + a is obtained by translating the graph of y = f(x) vertically by a units: up if a > 0 and down if a < 0.

cases.a: The graph of y = f(x - a) is the graph of y = f(x) translated a units to the right (to the left if a is negative).
cases.b: The graph of y = f(x-a) is obtained by translating the graph of y = f(x) horizontally by a units in the positive x-direction (to the right). This applies for any real constant a.

cases.a: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed; a horizontal line means the object is stationary.
cases.b: The gradient of a distance–time graph represents the object's speed: gradient = change in distance divided by change in time. For a curved graph, the gradient at a point gives the instantaneous speed at that time.
cases.note: B leaves out that a horizontal line means stationary

cases.a: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
cases.b: When you divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the inequality sign reverses direction. For example, if a < b and c < 0, then a/c > b/c.
cases.note: B covers dividing only, not multiplying (narrower)

cases.a: If a continuous function f has f(a) and f(b) of opposite signs, then f(x) = 0 has a solution between a and b.
cases.b: Since polynomials are continuous, if f(2)<0 and f(3)>0 then there is at least one real number c with 2<c<3 such that f(c)=0. This follows from the Intermediate Value Theorem.
cases.note: B is one example, not the general fact (narrower)

cases.a: Two straight lines are parallel exactly when they have the same gradient.
cases.b: Two straight lines are perpendicular exactly when their gradients multiply to -1.

cases.a: The graph of y = f(x - a) is the graph of y = f(x) translated a units to the right (to the left if a is negative).
cases.b: The graph of y = f(x - a) is the graph of y = f(x) translated a units to the left.

cases.a: The graph of y = f(x) + a is the graph of y = f(x) translated a units up (down if a is negative).
cases.b: The graph of y = f(x) + a is the graph of y = f(x) translated a units to the right.

cases.a: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
cases.b: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by any non-zero number reverses the inequality sign.
cases.note: drops the condition that the number is negative

cases.a: Two straight lines with gradients m and n (both non-zero) are perpendicular exactly when m × n = -1.
cases.b: Two straight lines with gradients m and n are perpendicular exactly when m × n = 1.

cases.a: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
cases.b: The area under a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.

cases.a: If a continuous function f has f(a) and f(b) of opposite signs, then f(x) = 0 has a solution between a and b.
cases.b: If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, then f(x) = 0 has a solution between a and b.
cases.note: leaves out the condition that f is continuous

cases.a: tan x = sin x / cos x, and cos 90° = 0, so tan 90° is undefined.
cases.b: tan 90° = 0, because sin 90° / cos 90° and cos 90° = 0.

cases.a: The graph of y = f(-x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in the y-axis.
cases.b: The graph of y = f(-x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in the x-axis.
